## What you just did, as diagrams
:::

```{=html}
<div id="m4-explain" class="lx-xgrid">
<div class="lx-fallback">
<dl class="lx-ideas">
<dt>One LP, three carriers</dt><dd>A balance row each hour for power, hydrogen and heat: 2,520 columns and 1,176 rows for a week.</dd>
<dt>Storage links the hours</dt><dd>Battery, tank and heat store each carry a level from hour to hour and end the week where they start.</dd>
<dt>Conversion couples the balances</dt><dd><span class="lx-term" data-term="sector-coupling">Coupling</span>: the electrolyzer turns 1 MWh into 17.5 kg; the heat pump turns it into 3 MWh of heat.</dd>
<dt>Where coupling pays</dt><dd>The <span class="lx-term" data-term="value-of-coupling">value of coupling</span>: heat coupling saves $21.0k in the winter week, $2.7k in summer: it needs heat demand at the same time as spare or cheap power.</dd>
<dt>Coupled prices</dt><dd>When the heat pump sets heat's price, heat is worth power's price ÷ 3: $40 ÷ 3 = $13.33 per MWh of heat.</dd>
</dl>
</div>
</div>
```

```{=html}
<div class="lx-deepers">
<details class="lx-deeper">
<summary><span class="k">Go deeper · Modeler</span>The plant's LP in algebra</summary>
<div class="lx-deeper-body">
```

For each hour $t = 0 \dots 167$ (one hour each, so MW over the hour is MWh), with $t-1$ read cyclically so every level ends the week where it starts:

$$\min \sum_t \Big( p_t\,(m_t - x_t) + 2.50\,r_t + 15\,b_t \Big)$$

$$
\begin{aligned}
x_t + c_t + y_t + h_t + u_t - m_t - d_t &= w_t && \text{(power)}\\
\tfrac{1000}{57}\,y_t + r_t + L_{t-1} - L_t &= 150 && \text{(hydrogen)}\\
3\,h_t + v_t - i_t + o_t + b_t = H_t, \quad 3\,h_t + v_t - i_t + o_t &\le 12 && \text{(heat; network)}\\
s_t = s_{t-1} + 0.83\,c_t - d_t, \quad Q_t &= (1-\lambda)\,Q_{t-1} + i_t - o_t && \text{(levels)}\\
400 \le L_t \le 4{,}000, \quad v_t \le 0.2\,y_t, \quad 0 \le y_t &\le 20 && \text{(limits)}
\end{aligned}
$$

| Symbol | Meaning | Unit |
|---|---|---|
| $x_t$, $m_t$ | sold to and bought from the grid, each at most 50 | MW |
| $p_t$ | Prairie Town's price | \$/MWh |
| $w_t$, $u_t$ | wind, and wind curtailed | MW |
| $c_t$, $d_t$, $s_t$ | battery charge, discharge (at most 20) and state of charge (at most 80) | MW, MWh |
| $y_t$ | electrolyzer power | MW |
| $L_t$, $r_t$ | hydrogen in the tank, hydrogen trucked in | kg |
| $h_t$ | heat pump power (at most 5) | MW |
| $v_t$, $b_t$, $H_t$ | heat recovered from the electrolyzer, from the boiler, and demanded | MW of heat |
| $i_t$, $o_t$, $Q_t$ | heat store charge, discharge and level (at most 60); $\lambda = 1 - 0.98^{1/24}$ | MW, MWh |

- **Duals.** The power row's dual, with its sign flipped, is power's marginal value in that hour; the hydrogen and heat rows' duals are the marginal costs of one more kg and one more MWh of heat, under this model's assumptions (fixed sizes, the modelled prices).
- **Unique or not.** Step 7 offers only hours where each dual is unique; the test checks that raising and lowering the hour's demand by 0.01 changes the cost at the same rate.
- **Size.** 2,520 columns and 1,176 rows; HiGHS solves it in tens of milliseconds.

```{=html}
</div>
</details>
<details class="lx-deeper">
<summary><span class="k">Go deeper · Modeler</span>Part-load limits: two LPs and a mixed-integer program</summary>
<div class="lx-deeper-body">
```

- **The exact rule.** Each hour the electrolyzer is on, between 15% and 100% of its size, or off: $3\,z_t \le y_t \le 20\,z_t$ with $z_t \in \{0, 1\}$, a [mixed-integer program]{.lx-term term="mixed-integer-program"} ([M2](m02-unit-commitment.html)).
- **Two LP stand-ins.** Drop the binary and allow any load (a relaxation, never dearer), or force $z_t = 1$ (always on, never cheaper).
- **This winter week:** relaxed −\$178.6k, exact −\$178.6k, forced on −\$172.7k. The exact cost lies between the two, as it must.
- **No prices from the MILP.** Its duals do not exist in the ordinary sense (§9.2); prices come from an LP with the on/off choices fixed.

```{=html}
</div>
</details>
<details class="lx-deeper">
<summary><span class="k">Go deeper</span>What this model leaves out</summary>
<div class="lx-deeper-body">
<ul>
<li>Sizes are given: choosing them is capacity expansion (<a href="m03-capacity-expansion.html">M3</a>), with a year of weeks linked as M3 links them.</li>
<li>Investment costs: the week's cost counts only buying, selling, trucks and the boiler.</li>
<li>Perfect foresight: the solver knows the whole week's wind and prices in advance.</li>
<li>Price-taking: the plant's sales do not move Prairie Town's price.</li>
<li>Electrochemistry, heat-network hydraulics and the tank's pressure: devices enter as efficiencies and limits.</li>
</ul>
</div>
</details>
</div>
```

## Check yourself
:::

```{=html}
<div class="lx-myths" data-quiz="m4-myth">
<div class="lx-qq" data-id="heat" data-answer="myth">
<p class="lx-qtext">Myth or fact? “A heat pump on a wind plant saves about the same in every season.”</p>
<ul class="lx-choices"><li data-value="myth">Myth</li><li data-value="fact">Fact</li></ul>
<details class="lx-answer"><summary>Answer</summary><p>Myth. Here heat coupling saves $21.0k in the winter week and $2.7k in the summer week: in summer there is little heat to make.</p></details>
</div>
<div class="lx-qq" data-id="load" data-answer="myth">
<p class="lx-qtext">Myth or fact? “Forcing an electrolyzer to stay on above its minimum load is the safe way to write the limit in an LP, and it costs nothing.”</p>
<ul class="lx-choices"><li data-value="myth">Myth</li><li data-value="fact">Fact</li></ul>
<details class="lx-answer"><summary>Answer</summary><p>Myth. It keeps the plan feasible but costs $6.0k more this winter week than the exact on/off model, which may switch the unit off.</p></details>
</div>
</div>

<div class="lx-quiz" data-quiz="m4">
<div class="lx-qq" data-id="kg" data-answer="b">
<p class="lx-qtext">The electrolyzer uses 57 kWh per kg. What coefficient links the power and hydrogen balances, in kg per MWh?</p>
<ul class="lx-choices"><li data-value="a">57</li><li data-value="b">17.5</li><li data-value="c">0.057</li><li data-value="d">1.75</li></ul>
<details class="lx-answer"><summary>Answer</summary><p>17.5: 1,000 ÷ 57 = 17.5 kg per MWh. 57 is kWh per kg, 0.057 is MWh per kg (the inverse), and 1.75 drops a factor of ten.</p></details>
</div>
</div>
```
